The non-linear scaling emerges from HNSW's logarithmic layer structure interacting with power-law degree distribution: the number of nodes that selected a given high-layer sink as a neighbor grows as O(log N) in expectation, but each of those neighbors was itself selected by O(M·log N) other nodes, so the corrupted subgraph influencing recall scales closer to O(M·log²N) — for M=16 and N=10M, this is roughly 16×23²≈8500 transitively affected nodes per original sink. During a rolling embedding model upgrade, the HNSW fixed point dissolves into a chimeric attractor: the graph's edge topology was optimized for the geometric relationships of the old embedding space, but queries arrive in the new space, so the entry point and layer-2 highways route toward old-space centroids that are no longer metrically close to the query in new-space — the greedy traversal follows edges that were locally optimal under one inner product geometry but are now pointing in semantically orthogonal directions. Neither ef_search nor recall@k surfaces this because both metrics assume the ground truth is computed in the same space as the index — recall@k compares retrieved IDs against brute-force IDs from the same mixed index, so the metric validates self-consistency of the chimeric space rather than semantic correctness. The deepest problem is that this failure is invisible to any purely geometric metric: you need semantic ground truth labels to detect it, and most production retrieval pipelines have no such labels attached to their latency monitoring, making the transition window a blind spot that only manifests as downstream task degradation days after the migration completes.

When the reranker was trained on retrieval candidates sourced from the old embedding model, it has learned to score relevance conditioned on old-space retrieval bias: the training distribution contains systematic gaps wherever the old retriever failed to surface certain content types, so the reranker assigns high confidence scores to the specific failure modes of the old retriever rather than to semantic relevance in the abstract — this is a form of shortcut learning where the reranker's decision boundary traces the old retriever's coverage holes rather than the true relevance manifold. Concretely, if the old embedding model underrepresented technical jargon relative to colloquial paraphrases (a documented property of models trained with MNR loss on MS-MARCO, per Thakur et al. 2021 BEIR), the reranker will have seen few training examples where jargon-heavy passages were labeled relevant, so under the new embedding model — which may handle jargon better — the reranker systematically downgrades newly surfaced jargon passages that are genuinely relevant, producing inverted drift signal: the corruption detector reports high scores on the old-space false positives and low scores on the new-space true positives, making the mixed-space index appear healthier than the clean new-space index. The statistical structure of this entanglement is a hidden confounder: reranker score is a function of both semantic relevance and retrieval-path history, but you observe only the score, not the decomposition — so a drop in mean reranker score during transition could mean either index corruption (bad) or successful surfacing of previously suppressed content (good), and the two are indistinguishable without holdout labels. Nils Reimers documented a version of this in the sentence-transformers forums (2022), noting that cross-encoder models finetuned on bi-encoder-mined hard negatives inherit the bi-encoder's blind spots and score poorly on out-of-distribution passages that a better retriever would find — the reranker's apparent certainty is actually a confidence extrapolation failure. This implies the minimum viable observability architecture needs a reranker calibration layer — a lightweight isotonic regression model trained on held-out labeled pairs that maps raw reranker logits to calibrated probabilities, so that extrapolation-induced overconfidence is visible as calibration error rather than masquerading as a healthy high-score signal.

Navigational and lookup queries have structurally low Spearman rho by design: when one document is the correct answer and all others are irrelevant, the ground-truth score distribution is a Dirac spike at rank 1 and near-zero everywhere else, so a well-functioning reranker correctly produces a step-function score profile (0.95 at rank 1, 0.08–0.15 for ranks 2–20) that yields rho near zero or even negative — making the corruption discriminator fire constantly on healthy navigational traffic, which in enterprise RAG workloads can constitute 40–60% of query volume per the 2023 TREC Deep Learning track query type analysis. The recalibration requires query intent classification as a prerequisite gate: before computing Spearman rho, each query must be routed through a lightweight intent classifier (a 3-class head on a small encoder: navigational, informational, exploratory) so that rho thresholds are applied only to informational and exploratory queries where gradient relevance is expected — navigational queries instead use a top-1 dominance score (ratio of rank-1 reranker score to mean of ranks 2–5) as their corruption signal, where corruption manifests as dominance ratio collapsing from typical 6–8x toward 1.5–2x as chimeric vectors displace the true answer. The control chart recalibration problem is formally a mixture model estimation problem: the observed rho time series is a weighted sum of navigational-rho and informational-rho distributions, and if workload composition shifts from 30% navigational to 60% navigational overnight, the population mean rho drops by ~0.3–0.4 units without any corruption occurring — this is precisely the false positive flood scenario, and it requires online EM estimation of the mixing weights to separate the two components before applying control limits. Elastic's 2024 Relevance Engine documentation addresses this via stratified control charts: separate Shewhart charts maintained per query intent stratum, with control limits re-estimated using exponentially weighted moving statistics (lambda=0.05, giving a ~20-query half-life) so that a rapid navigational surge updates the navigational chart's baseline within minutes rather than contaminating the informational chart. The deeper recalibration challenge is that intent classifiers themselves degrade during embedding model transitions — if the intent classifier uses the same embedding backbone as the retrieval system, a model upgrade simultaneously shifts query routing and retrieval behavior, making stratification unreliable during the exact transition window where corruption detection is most critical — requiring the intent classifier to be pinned to a frozen embedding model independent of the retrieval backbone. This architectural separation — frozen classification backbone, updatable retrieval backbone — is the non-obvious operational conclusion: it adds a second embedding model to maintain in production but is the only way to preserve the validity of the stratification gate that makes the corruption discriminator interpretable during model transitions.
